introduction.text: The Catacombe di San Callisto is a major Roman catacomb on the Appian Way, notable for its Crypt of the Popes and its extensive underground network of burial chambers that span several centuries.

history.description: The catacomb was originally established by future Pope Callixtus I, a deacon of Rome, under the direction of Pope Zephyrinus, expanding pre‑existing early Christian hypogea.
The Crypt of the Popes contains the tombs of nine popes from the 2nd to the 4th centuries, including Pontian, Anterus, Fabian, Lucius I, Eutychian, and Sixtus II.
Pope Damasus I built a staircase in the 4th century to provide access to the region of the Popes.
Relics from the crypt were translated to churches of Rome, with the final wave of translations carried out under Pope Sergius II in the 9th century.
The catacomb and its crypt were rediscovered in 1854 by the Italian archaeologist Giovanni Battista de Rossi.

design.description: The catacomb comprises five underground levels, with roughly twenty kilometres of passageways, covering about fifteen hectares, and containing an estimated half a million bodies.

art.description: Early Christian paintings and frescoes in the catacomb depict biblical scenes such as baptism, the Eucharist, and the Good Shepherd, and include Greek inscriptions on walls.
